title: Financial Modelling, Lesson 4: supporting schedules - depreciation and working capital
subtitle: The two supporting schedules that decide whether your cash flow is trustworthy
whyItMatters: The three main statements cannot run on their own without the supporting schedules behind them. The depreciation schedule and the working capital schedule are the two most important - they turn operating assumptions into concrete numbers that flow into the P&L, the balance sheet and the cash flow statement alike.
openingQuestion: What is a working capital schedule in a model usually forecast from?
openingOptions: A fixed percentage of total assets
Turnover days: DIO, DSO and DPO tied to revenue and COGS
Exactly last year's balance, held constant through every forecast year
explanation: Working capital is forecast through turnover days: inventory on DIO (days inventory outstanding, tied to COGS), receivables on DSO (days sales outstanding, tied to revenue), payables on DPO (days payable outstanding, tied to COGS). This keeps working capital scaling automatically with the size of the business.

realWorldExample.description: A company that doubles revenue usually sees inventory and receivables roughly double as well. If the model holds working capital constant, the forecast cash flow comes out unrealistically attractive. This is why so many fast-growing businesses still run out of cash - the 'growing broke' phenomenon that a model has to be able to show.

quiz.question: What is the job of the depreciation schedule in a model?
options: Computing the corporate income tax payable each period
Computing interest expense on the average debt balance
Tracking cost, adding CapEx, deducting depreciation
Forecasting the revenue generated by the fixed asset base
quiz.explanation: The depreciation schedule is the fixed asset register: opening balance + CapEx − depreciation for the period = closing balance, feeding straight into the balance sheet. Tax and interest have their own schedules driven by different inputs, and revenue is forecast from operating drivers rather than from the asset base - a factory does not produce sales in proportion to its book value.

quiz.question: What does DSO rising from 30 to 60 days mean for cash flow?
options: Cash flow improves because more goods are being sold
It affects profit only, and does not touch cash flow
No effect at all since revenue for the period is unchanged
Cash flow worsens because money is tied up twice as long
quiz.explanation: A longer DSO means customers are paying more slowly, so receivables swell and cash sits outside the business. Note that DSO says nothing about how much was sold - revenue can be flat while collection deteriorates - and this is a pure cash effect: under accrual accounting the profit was already recognised at the point of sale, so the income statement does not move at all.

quiz.question: How should CapEx be forecast in a model?
options: Tied to growth, as a percentage of revenue
Always set to 0 to keep the forecast model simple
Exactly equal to depreciation every year, in all cases
Equal to net profit for that same forecast year
quiz.explanation: CapEx should reflect the real requirement: maintaining existing capacity plus expansion investment where the model forecasts volume growth. Setting it to zero eventually shrinks the asset base to nothing, tying it mechanically to depreciation assumes no growth at all, and net profit is an accounting outcome with no causal link to what the business needs to spend on assets.

quiz.question: Why is it the CHANGE in working capital that feeds cash flow, rather than the balance?
options: Because the balance already appears on the balance sheet
Because cash flow measures flow; a balance is a stock
Because working capital is always 0 at each period end
Because accounting standards require that presentation
quiz.explanation: The cash flow statement records movement. Inventory of 100bn in two consecutive periods generates no cash flow at all; only when it rises to 130bn does a further 30bn of cash get tied up. The fact that the balance also appears on the balance sheet is true but is not the reason - the two statements simply answer different questions, one about position and one about movement.

quiz.question: Why are trade payables tied to COGS rather than to revenue?
options: Because COGS is always smaller than revenue, so the days figure comes out steadier
Because accounting standards require payables to be presented alongside COGS
Because it arises from buying materials, not from selling goods
Because revenue has already been used for the receivables line
quiz.explanation: Every working capital line has to be tied to the flow that generates it: receivables to revenue because that is money customers owe, inventory and payables to COGS because those are the goods and the money owed to suppliers. Tie it to the wrong base and the days figure still computes but no longer means anything at all.

keyTakeaways: Depreciation schedule: opening balance + CapEx − depreciation = closing balance
Working capital is forecast on turnover days DIO/DSO/DPO, so it scales with the business automatically
Only the CHANGE in working capital between two periods flows into cash flow, not the balance
Holding working capital fixed while revenue grows sharply produces an unrealistic forecast cash flow

practicePrompt.question: Revenue rises from 500bn to 750bn. DSO stays at 60 days. What happens to receivables, and what is the effect on cash flow?
options: Unchanged, because the DSO assumption itself is unchanged
Up from about 82bn to 123bn, cutting cash flow by roughly 41bn
Down, because the company is now selling more successfully
It doubles, because revenue rose by one and a half times
practicePrompt.explanation: Receivables = revenue × DSO / 365. Before: 500 × 60/365 ≈ 82bn. After: 750 × 60/365 ≈ 123bn. That is a 41bn increase, and a rise in current assets means cash flow falls by the same 41bn. Even though collection efficiency has not deteriorated at all, growth still pulls cash out of the business.

summary.keyIdea: Supporting schedules turn operating assumptions into figures that flow into all three statements
summary.commonMistake: Holding working capital fixed while revenue grows, which makes the forecast cash flow look artificially good.
summary.action: Compute the actual DIO, DSO and DPO for a real company from its most recent financial statements.

application.title: Compute the real turnover days
application.message: Take a listed company's statements and compute DIO = inventory × 365 / COGS, DSO = receivables × 365 / revenue, DPO = payables × 365 / COGS. These are exactly the assumptions you will use to forecast.
application.secondary: Compare them against industry peers to see which figure is the unusual one.

sections.text: The three main statements are the part everyone looks at, but what makes them run is the supporting schedules behind them. The two most important: depreciation and working capital.
The depreciation schedule - the fixed asset register

sections.title: The roll-forward structure
sections.equation: Closing fixed assets = Opening fixed assets + CapEx − Depreciation for the period

example.title: Why this structure matters
example.calculation: Depreciation → P&L (expense) and CF (added back); CapEx → CF (investing outflow); Closing balance → balance sheet
example.result: One schedule supplying figures to all three statements
example.explanation: This is why the depreciation schedule has to be built separately rather than scattered through formulas - one single source feeding three places.

sections.text: The working capital schedule - where growth eats cash

Working capital is forecast on turnover days rather than absolute amounts, so it scales automatically with the size of the business. **Receivables = Revenue × DSO / 365**; **Inventory = COGS × DIO / 365**; **Payables = COGS × DPO / 365**.

sections.label: Growth always drains cash
sections.text: Even when operating efficiency is unchanged, rising revenue drags inventory and receivables up with it, pulling cash out of the business. A model that holds working capital fixed hides that risk - the very risk that has bankrupted many fast-growing companies.
How growth eats cash, in numbers

Revenue 1,000bn, COGS 700bn. Days: receivables 60, inventory 45, payables 30. Working capital = 1,000×60/365 + 700×45/365 − 700×30/365 = 164 + 86 − 58 ≈ 193bn. Next year revenue grows 30% to 1,300bn, COGS rises in step to 910bn and the days are unchanged: 214 + 112 − 75 ≈ 251bn. A gap of 58bn - that is cash the business has to find purely to fund the growth, before any fixed asset investment is even discussed.

sections.label: Why a profitable business can still die of cash
sections.text: If net profit in that growth year is 50bn while working capital absorbs 58bn, operating cash flow is already negative despite a very handsome income statement. The faster the growth, the harder the drain - and that is how a rapidly expanding company can go bankrupt while posting a profit every quarter. A model that forecasts working capital as a fixed number will never show this; it only appears once working capital is tied to revenue through turnover days.

lines: Supporting schedules are where operating assumptions turn into real money.
